props.title: Control
props.initialSlug: Haunting portrait of Joy Division's Ian Curtis

sections.content: Control (2007) stands as one of the most compelling music biopics ever made, shot in stark black-and-white by photographer Anton Corbijn who actually photographed Joy Division in their heyday. The film captures Ian Curtis's short, intense life with an authenticity missing from most rock movies. Sam Riley's portrayal of Curtis digs deep into the singer's epilepsy, depression, and creative fire without romanticizing his struggles. Like 24 Hour Party People (2002), it explores Manchester's explosive post-punk scene, but where that film went for wild energy, Control maintains a haunting restraint that mirrors Joy Division's atmospheric sound.

sections.content: The film belongs to a vital wave of 2000s music biopics that rejected the formulaic Walk the Line (2005) approach. Like I'm Not There (2007), which fractured Bob Dylan into multiple personas, Control finds fresh ways to explore an artist's life. The domestic scenes between Curtis and his wife Deborah (Samantha Morton) feel devastatingly real, while the concert recreations capture Joy Division's hypnotic power. Corbijn's background photographing the band gives the film an insider's eye - every frame could be an iconic rock photo.

Beyond Curtis's story, Control documents a pivotal moment when British post-punk was reshaping popular music. Like This Is England (2006) and The Filth and the Fury (2000), it shows how economic despair in late-70s Britain fueled explosive creativity. The film's depiction of Manchester's grey industrial landscape helps us understand the environment that produced Joy Division's dark, revolutionary sound. sections.content: Control helped inspire a new generation of innovative music films like Amy (2015) and Montage of Heck (2015), documentaries that use intimate archival footage to create deeply personal portraits. The film's influence can also be seen in recent biopics like Stardust (2020) and Creation Stories (2021), which focus on specific pivotal moments rather than trying to cover entire careers. Its success proved audiences would embrace unconventional approaches to telling musicians' stories.
